You're unlikely to lose or fail during this period of adjustment.
MachineHandbookEntry|FailedAttemptsAreHo: Failed Attempts Are How You Probe
You won't be immediately successful in some combat situations. Many fights on the path to your goals will be too hard to complete on a first pass.

Using StreetSense or Contemplation, you can detect side activities. Strengthen your forces by completing those. Especially the Contemplations.
A first pass at a difficult encounter can also give you ideas on how to refit your forces to better tackle that specific scenario.
MachineHandbookEntry|ContemplationsSomet:
Once you have a shell company in chapter two and onward, there are a variety of opportunities that may be noticed only by having the right kind of scientific staff on hand.
You are something of a scientist yourself -- well, to be honest, you're more of an engineer -- but specialists will notice things that you never would.

Once you can afford it, building a single structure for employing each kind of scientist (and having them staffed!) will ensure you never miss anything.
And if you can't afford it... have you SEEN the prices of water lately? Especially if you sell to the wealthy, you can ensure you have enough funds to last for years.
MachineHandbookEntry|TheUpperRightCheckL: The Task Stack Is The Key Path

The task stack, in the form of a checklist in the upper right corner of your view, is the key path forward.
Later on, as you choose your own paths, that will still be true.
If there is Dialog Available, then that's the path forward.

When you're stuck on the key path, or just want to explore, check out Contemplations to find side content that will help you become more powerful.
If you run out of side content, don't forget to go back to the key path. The upper right corner is your most important set of items.
MachineHandbookEntry|BulkAndroids|descri:
You can't be everywhere at once. More importantly, you don't want to be.
Up until now, your focus has been your standard androids. They are part of your consciousness. Now you can add in bulk minions that act on their own.
MachineHandbookEntry|BulkAndroids|strate:
Not all android classes can be used in a bulk format -- some are just too specialized.
You can have more bulks than standard units, and they don't cost any mental energy when they make their attacks per turn. They DO cost mental energy to deploy or reposition, however.
They may lack the abilities and finesse of your standard units, but they make up for it with numbers. They tend to be best as an occupying force that protects an area.
MachineHandbookEntry|WorkerAndroids|desc:
Worker androids are very distant from your consciousness. These are tied to specific buildings that spawn them, and what the workers do is based on the structure that spawns them.
Workers do not have any sort of generalized cap, do not cost mental energy to deploy, cannot use equipment, and only come in three flavors: Predator, Sledge, and PMC Impostor.
MachineHandbookEntry|WorkerAndroids|stra:
When you have a structure that uses Worker Androids, you will first need to build Android Frames of the appropriate types. Using the Workers tab in Command Mode, you can also disable specific kinds of workers from spawning, if you wish.
What each worker type does depends on the building that spawns them. Each building uses them very differently, but explains how they are used.
MachineHandbookEntry|DealsAreSoftPower|d:
All that manufacturing power at your fingertips, and nobody to benefit. Well, humans are really into a lot of the stuff you make.
Deals are a way of using your manufacturing capabilities to influence the world around you -- or get something you can't get any other way.
MachineHandbookEntry|DealsAreSoftPower|s: All deals give you some sort of passive benefit. If you go into the Resources window, and then go to the Deals tab, you can often increase the intensity of the deal to get a stronger benefit, if you have extra of the resource in question.
MachineHandbookEntry|ClearancesAreContex:
The android forms designed by humans all have level 1 (Sight) clearance.
They lose this when they're marked defective.

Consider your options in StreetSense for removing the Marked Defective badge.
You can visit a licensing agency and pay a fee on behalf of 'your employer,' or you can grab a replacement registration from another android.
MachineHandbookEntry|SuspiciousAndroidsI:
When your androids are blending in, they're anonymous among the many androids in the city. 
But a pattern has been noticed -- ever since the eruption of your tower more androids have been acting suspiciously.

If you get into a fight with military or security forces, and you don't wipe them out, they're going to start targeting buildings around your tower.
For some reason, your tower itself seems off limits at the moment. But any freaky metallic buildings around it are fair game.
MachineHandbookEntry|NotAllEnemiesGoAway: Not All Enemies Go Away After Combat

If you lose a combat, even one where you were just probing to check enemy capabilities, pay close attention to which units leave -- saying their job is done.
The really big nasty ones tend to be needed elsewhere, but the smaller and mid-scale units will often hang around.

One of two things will then happen.
If they're defense-oriented, they may hang around the area they were sent to guard -- indefinitely. If you're returning to try that combat again, be sure to clear out those units before resuming the main encounter.
If they're aggressive then they'll quickly advance toward any freaky metallic structures you've built. Be prepared to intercept them.
MachineHandbookEntry|EliminateEnemiesLef:
If enemies spawned due to an activity you were engaged in, clear them out.
If they're defending an area you need to pass through later, that could be a problem. Or if they're waiting until one of your units becomes marked defective, you may get ambushed.

You don't gain anything from killing these units, and you won't trigger more units to spawn by killing them.
What you do accomplish is making sure that they don't re-engage with you at an inconvenient time.
If you're already pretty experienced and you want to leave enemies who might later fight a mutual foe, then by all means feel free to do so.
Or leave them if you're just not going back to that part of the map for a long while. You aren't the maid.
MachineHandbookEntry|YourMilitarySecrets: Vorsiber hackers have stolen some of your military secrets! This gives them and all of their allies a small attack bonus against your units.

It's a very small bonus, not reflected in any of their visible stats, but it is cumulative in this timeline. You can see the total number of secrets stolen in the city statistics tab of the information window.
Be sure and stop their hackers to keep them from gaining any further advantage. Once your Neural Secret Protection has reached 0 on a vulnerable building, the hackers can just keep looting it for more bonuses against you.
If you absolutely have to, you can scrap or disable the building to remove their ability to get more bonuses. As soon as you rebuild or turn it back on, they'll be back -- just make sure you are better prepared.
MachineHandbookEntry|ExoCorpStoleMilitar: ExoCorp hackers have stolen some of your military secrets! This gives all ExoCorp units an attack bonus against your units.

It's a moderate bonus, not reflected in any of their visible stats, but it is cumulative in this timeline. You can see the total number of secrets stolen in the city statistics tab of the information window.
Be sure and stop their hackers to keep them from gaining any further advantage. Once your Firewall Strength has reached 0 on a vulnerable building, the hackers can just keep looting it for more bonuses against you.
MachineHandbookEntry|YourFirstShellCompa:
Now that you have a shell company, you can build the Senior Technician, who can do a variety of contemplations unavailable to the rest of your forces.
There may not be a huge number of opportunities just yet, but you can generate some wealth and hire some scientists and see if they produce anything of note.

As you progress further into different project chains in chapter two and onward, shell companies become critical.
Outside of those scenarios they are still highly useful, largely as a means to buy and sell resources in a way you otherwise could not.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitCaps|descriptio:
Each android takes up a certain amount of capacity, which determines how many you can have at once.
Basic units like Technicians use 4 capacity, while more advanced androids may require 16 or more.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitCaps|strategy_t:
If you exceed the limit, you won't be able to deploy or create new androids until you scrap existing ones to free up space.
You can check your current android count and limit at the top of the FORCES panel (e.g., 'Androids 46/48'). The cap can be increased through upgrades and other mechanics.
Vehicles and Mechs work essentially the same way, but have their own independent caps.
MachineHandbookEntry|ProjectsWithStreetS:
There are a variety of projects that involve you taking a series of actions in StreetSense. Doing work, helping people, hurting people, examining locations, and so on.
Except in a few cases, the actual result is the same regardless of which actions you take. In other words, any combination of actions you take will complete the project, most of the time.

This might sound strange, but you can probably relate this to some experiences in your own life. Sometimes the result is inevitable.
In those cases, what changes is YOU. Doing things one way or another leads to changes in yourself -- or in this case, in your units, equipment, or structures.
So while the primary result may be a given, the secondary benefits vary massively. Smart choices that fit your strategy can have a big impact on your long-term plans.
MachineHandbookEntry|MeleeLeaps|descript: Your units have attack ranges lower than their move ranges. However, they also have superhuman speed. If you initiate an attack beyond their attack range, they will execute a leaping melee attack.
MachineHandbookEntry|MeleeLeaps|strategy: These melee leaps do half damage, but follow-up attacks will do full damage.
MachineHandbookEntry|TakingCover|descrip: Check out the tooltip for Take Cover in your ability bar, slot 4. It's important.
MachineHandbookEntry|TakingCover|strateg: Darting in and out of the range of enemies uses a lot of Mental Energy and exposes you to attacks of opportunity.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitsCanReload|disp: Units Can Recharge To Take More Actions
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitsCanReload|desc: Check out the tooltip for Recharge in your ability bar, slot 1. This is how you balance your global Mental Energy versus AP of individual units.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitsCanReload|stra:
Hover over the AP meter at the center of the radial menu for extra details.		  
You can see extra details about Mental Energy right next to that, or also in the middle of the radial menu.
MachineHandbookEntry|VehiclesInCombat|de: Your flying vehicles occupy a wide range of combat roles: support, logistics, fire suppression, stealth, and raw firepower.
MachineHandbookEntry|VehiclesInCombat|st: You'll tend to have fewer vehicles than you will androids, but they'll often be critical to combined-arms battle plans. Don't ignore them!
MachineHandbookEntry|OrderOfCombat|descr:
During your turn, the units that are part of your consciousness are able to act faster than enemy forces can react (attacks of opportunity aside).
After you proceed to the next turn, all other units -- enemy and allied NPCs, your bulk and worker units, any captured troops you have, and so on -- all act at the same time.
MachineHandbookEntry|OrderOfCombat|strat:
During the NPC phase, everyone attacks at once. This means that your bulks and workers cannot prevent enemy damage or enemy actions, since they all act at once.
Any NPCs that survive the attack phase then get to do another action, which is typically movement. This happens after the attacks resolved.
MachineHandbookEntry|UsingBulksDefensive:
Bulk units and captured units are hard to use defensively, because of the order of combat. They can't prevent any enemy damage if enemies are already aiming at them.
In order to use these kinds of units in a defensive fashion, two things need to be true: the enemies must be approaching from a distance, and your bulks or captured troops must be positioned in a manner to intercept the enemies before the enemies are in firing range of the targets you want to protect.
You can always rely on repair spiders and crabs to simply repair damage after it happens, if you need to.
MachineHandbookEntry|WhatMarksYouDefecti:
An individual unit will be marked defective when it physically attacks members of the military, SecForce, or similar. Generally anyone working for Vorsiber or a federated corporation (fedcorp).
Morale-based attacks will not cause this, nor will physically attacking citizens, criminals, religions, cults, or similar.
Demolishing very large buildings using explosives will get you marked defective, as will certain other very-scary abilities.

A defective unit isn't a crisis. It means that all military and SecForce units who are not on permanent guard duty will target that unit, but guards will continue to ignore it.
On the other hand, it does mean that unit's ability to blend in is gone, which can be problematic if you need to sneak into a restricted area to do a contemplation.
MachineHandbookEntry|WhatCountsAsMurder|: What Counts As Murder? (For Goal Purposes)

Murder includes: killing non-combatants, destroying civilian-occupied buildings (even by accident), attempting to kill underage combatants, and (almost) any action or event that specifically uses the word 'Murder' instead of 'Kill.'
Not murder: killing armed enemies in battle, deaths of displaced humans from exposure, deaths caused by third parties.

You can see your list of murders, if there are any, in the Action Statistics tab of the Information window.
There is one (intentionally) misleading category, called 'Androids Murdered For Registration.' This uses the word murder, but it does not count against you for goal purposes. May be some deeper story significance there...
Mulching humans into 'canned protein' is also something you would think is murder, but it turns out that it doesn't count if you do it in a businesslike manner. Who knew.
MachineHandbookEntry|KillingHackers|disp: Why Can I Only Kill Hackers Sometimes?
MachineHandbookEntry|KillingHackers|desc:
It depends on what the hacker is doing at the time.
If the hacker is only suspicious of your presence but hasn't fully detected your unit, attacking them sets off an alarm. This triggers security measures, causing your infiltrator to take damage from the alerted forces inside the building. These are always secretive Infiltration missions -- if someone realizes an intruder is inside, everything escalates.
MachineHandbookEntry|KillingHackers|stra: In cases where you can freely kill hackers, they're not actively tracking an infiltrator inside a high-security area. Instead, they're attacking through network-based warfare, which means alarms aren't a factor. You're in some degree of open warfare with them, so the rules are different.
MachineHandbookEntry|TargetingUplink|des:
This equipment is a bit complicated. On its own, it doesn't do anything. It exists solely to use in combination with the Designate Coordinated Attack consumable item.
Designate Coordinated Attack can be used by 'support units,' which you can find by using the second dropdown on the Hardware screen.
When a support unit uses Designate Coordinated Attack, then any Bulk and regular units that have Targeting Uplink installed will automatically fire on the target that the support unit designates.
MachineHandbookEntry|TargetingUplink|str:
This is very powerful! Each regular unit will use one Action Point when doing this, but bulk units will not. Any attacks that would require Mental Energy will be skipped.
Only units with Targeting Uplink equipped who are also within firing range of the support unit designating the attack will fire; however, the strength of the Targeting Uplink adds to their normal firing range for this purpose only.
MachineHandbookEntry|TalkToEnemies|displ: How Do I Talk To Enemies Instead Of Shooting Them?
MachineHandbookEntry|TalkToEnemies|descr:
Some androids have the Force Conversation ability, allowing them to initiate discussion with enemies -- but only if the enemy is willing to talk. Hovering over an enemy will show how many conversations you can force with them, if any.
Most enemies cannot be engaged in conversation, while some can be approached multiple times.
MachineHandbookEntry|TalkToEnemies|strat: If your android lacks this ability by default, you can add it in the Loadout window, where you set equipment and abilities for your unit types.
MachineHandbookEntry|AttacksOfOpportunit: If you move one of your units away from an enemy that is actively targeting it, that enemy will get a free attack for a small randomized percentage of its normal damage.

To minimize this, consider the order in which you move your units -- or consider staying where you are and taking cover.
If you are trespassing, and the guards are targeting you but the alarm is not active, then you can move laterally without triggering an attack of opportunity.
To do so, move out of the restricted area, but still within the range of the units targeting you. At that point, since the non-alarmed guards won't target you anymore, you can freely move away without being attacked.
MachineHandbookEntry|SquadsOfHumans|desc: Most human-scale NPC units are squads rather than individual units (that is, each individual displayed unit on the map is a full squad). Hover over them for more details.
MachineHandbookEntry|SquadsOfHumans|stra:
Squad members die proportionally to the damage taken.
As members of the squad die, stats that come from the collective (such as attack power, strength, intimidation, etc.) are reduced.
Stats that are not collective (such as attack range and movement range) are not reduced.
MachineHandbookEntry|SquadsOfAndroids|de: Squads of robots are substantially more robust than human squads.
MachineHandbookEntry|SquadsOfAndroids|st:
Robotic members of a squad are not killed until the entire squad goes down.
This means that stats such as attack power and strength are not reduced as they take damage.
MachineHandbookEntry|VehicleCrews|descri: Most vehicles have a human crew. As the vehicle takes damage, crew members die.
MachineHandbookEntry|VehicleCrews|strate:
Key vehicle stats, such as drone resistance, rely on the crew. So a damaged vehicle will be more vulnerable to drone incursions.
However, most vehicle stats, including attack power, are not reduced by crew deaths.
MachineHandbookEntry|SomeEnemiesAreWeakF: Some enemies take extra damage if you attack them from behind.

If they are actively targeting your unit, you won't be able to get behind them, since they rotate to face your unit as soon as you move.
In these cases, you'll need to have two of your units work together.
Some enemies take extra damage if you attack them from higher than their current location.
You may need to draw an enemy close to tall buildings, or fly higher than the target using your own aircraft.
MachineHandbookEntry|MostEnemiesHaveNoSp: Most Enemies Have No Spatial Weaknesses

Most enemies are not extra-weak to attacks from behind or above.
Your units are NEVER spatially extra weak.

For those enemies that do have spatial weaknesses, the weakness info is shown in the attack damage prediction tooltip by your mouse cursor. It also shows if you are getting the bonus. 
If a strong enemy has no spatial weakness, consider applying status effects on yourself or inflicting them on your foes.
MachineHandbookEntry|SomeHaveArmorPlatin:
Armor plating is extremely effective, but also expensive. Most units won't have it.
Your ability to deal meaningful damage to armored enemies drops dramatically.

In order to bypass these heavy defenses, you will need to develop an effective form of armor piercing.
A stroke of inspiration on that topic will occur to you when the time is right.
MachineHandbookEntry|LightReinforcements:
Military transports bring reinforcements from large military bases to smaller outposts, farms, and so forth.
If you see them coming, you can shoot them down to prevent the reinforcement from happening.
These reinforcements are always ground troops and similar, never mechs.
MachineHandbookEntry|HeavyReinforcements:
High-Altitude Military Transports bring reinforcements from outside the city, and deposit them in the largest military bases.
These have an incredibly high amount of armor, so you're unlikely to be able to shoot them down. But you can note their movement to predict when reinforcements happen.
Any facility that has mechs as guards will get reinforced in this way. The transport brings in both mechs and ground troops.
MachineHandbookEntry|Feats|description:
Feats are special talents held by a unit, which are passively applied.
Technicians have a stun effect from all of their attacks, and some enemies have a bonus against structures, for example.
MachineHandbookEntry|Feats|strategy_tip:
Feats have a numeric value to them, so one unit may be stronger at a feat than another. Feats are always good for the unit that has them.
Feats can come from equipment, or the stance of a unit, or just be intrinsically part of a unit.
The amount for a feat does not stack; if multiple sources provide a feat to a unit, then the highest value is used, rather than the combined value.
MachineHandbookEntry|Perks|description:
Perks are long-lasting status effects of a unit that tend to be good, but don't have to be. They are things like 'Blending In,' 'Innately Alarming,' or the military perk Achilles.
These make a unit less-noticeable, highly-noticeable, or change how they exploit enemy weaknesses, respectively.
MachineHandbookEntry|Perks|strategy_tip:
Perks are on/off, so you either have that perk or do not.
Perks can come from equipment, or the stance of a unit, or just be intrinsically part of a unit. Some badges or perks block other perks.
MachineHandbookEntry|Badges|description:
Badges are status effects that are in no way related to the unit's stance or equipment, and are never intrinsic to a unit.
They can be good, bad, or neutral; but one way or another, they are related to the history of that unit, and how that relates to its current state.
MachineHandbookEntry|Badges|strategy_tip:
One example badge notes that a transport vehicle has been emptied, and the transport loses that badge the next time it fills up.
The most common badge is that an android has been marked defective by the authorities -- that can also be scrubbed through various means.
MachineHandbookEntry|TemporaryStatusEffe:
Temporary Status Effects have a numeric intensity, but they also only last for a few turns.
Temporary status effects are often negative debuffs, like 'that unit is on fire' or 'that unit is distracted,' and the intensity says how much.
But they can also be positive buffs, like 'temporarily has armor-plating-piercing', and again the intensity says how much.
Your primary means of applying status effects to your own units or enemies is by use of Consumable Items.
MachineHandbookEntry|HeroUnits|descripti:
Hero units are ones that have been upgraded with unique badges that make them more powerful than the regular units of their type. If a hero unit dies, it is gone forever, so treat them with extra care.
Hero units are typically introduced once you reach Intelligence Class 5. However, there are a few you can get access to earlier than this.
MachineHandbookEntry|HeroUnits|strategy_: Once you have hero units, it's time to consider using the Android Torpor StreetSense action if you temporarily do not need one of them.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitEquipment|descr:
Your units have an array of equipment available including primary weapons, secondary weapons, armor, and augments.
Units fire every weapon they have, all at once, whenever they attack.
MachineHandbookEntry|UnitEquipment|strat:
All equipment stats stack and the only cost is a cooldown during which you cannot change that specific equipment slot again. Loadouts are set per unit class.
When you find yourself in a new and dangerous situation, consider taking a moment to alter your loadouts.
MachineHandbookEntry|LoadoutsArePerClass:
Broad unit classes can be configured with a set of equipment and abilities.
Units within a class all share that loadout.

Individual units have a low rate of survival. You would not want to configure them individually.
As you discover or invent more unit classes, you'll have greater flexibility in running multiple loadouts side by side.
MachineHandbookEntry|LoadoutChangesAreFr: Changes to a unit class's loadout are free in every sense.
After you make a change to a slot on a class, there is a cooldown before you can make another change again. This is to prevent you from micromanaging during combat.
MachineHandbookEntry|SortingUnitsByCapab: To find a unit with a high amount of a certain stat, look at the Unit Analysis tab of the Hardware screen.
Use filters to narrow down to what you are looking for.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceRange|des: Units that are not invisible provide deterrence to all structures and flags within their attack range.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceRange|str: Territory control flags and some structures require deterrence to avoid constant attacks.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceDensity|d: Whenever possible, build flags or buildings that require deterrence close together.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceDensity|s:
The amount of deterrence required does not increase when you build densely.
Some advanced structures will need to be spread out -- but you may find ways to stack them closely. Take any advantage you can get.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceFormula|d: Deterrence is calculated from the attack power, health, and intimidation of your units.
MachineHandbookEntry|DeterrenceFormula|s: In case you are curious, the specific formula is A = (power + health + 5x armor + 3x piercing). Result = A + ( (intimidation / 150) * A ).
MachineHandbookEntry|GatherSpotsAreInfin: Unless otherwise specified, a resource gather spot will give a fixed amount of resources indefinitely.

There are some cases where previously-infinite resources suddenly start running dry due to a change in the state of the city.
This is typically either related to enemy action, or some major choice you made. This will tell you what's happening if it does.
MachineHandbookEntry|ResourceStorage|des:
As you progress, you'll find more esoteric resources to store.
If you gain a resource that you don't have proper storage for, this Excess will be kept in ad-hoc storage -- but you'll need a real storage facility before you can use them.
MachineHandbookEntry|ResourceStorage|str:
Losing a storage facility will also result in a loss of whatever it was storing.
Storage of a resources is always evenly divided between any buildings of the type that can store it, so if you have two buildings, each will always contain half.
Also, some of these things explode...
MachineHandbookEntry|ResourcesAreCentral:
Most resources require storage structures to increase your cap of that resource.
But you don't have to worry about the logistics of resources moving into that storage, or between structures that use them.

If one of your storage structures is destroyed, you lose a portion of the resources it holds.
The amount always assumes that each resource is evenly-distributed. So if that was your only structure, you lose everything. If you had two, you lose half.
MachineHandbookEntry|ResourcesDisplayIsC:
In the upper left corner, are resources related to your current project(s), and whatever building you have selected or have your mouse over.
You can also Pin a resource to the top bar by clicking it in the inventory window.

There are a lot of resources, and most of them do not need to be watched unless there is a problem.
To get an overview of how things are doing, go to your Inventory screen and look at either the Ledger, or the TPS Reports, or both.
MachineHandbookEntry|TerritoryControl|de:
On occasion, you'll want to take control of the resources in an area. From the build menu, you can place a flag for certain resources -- but only one of each type.
Once the flag is in place, send your units, prepare your defenses, and then select the flag.
On the bottom-left info panel (while the flag is selected) you can activate or deactivate it to assert or relinquish your claim to the local resource.
MachineHandbookEntry|TerritoryControl|st:
The owners of the resource you are trying to control won't like this.
Any time you activate the flag, they will send a strike force.
If you have enough deterrence in the local area (or are using Simplified Defenses), they won't come back.
MachineHandbookEntry|ConstructionIsRelax: You will not be punished later for building your structures 'in the wrong spot.'
Later in the game, the position of specific advanced buildings will have restrictions, but right now location isn't important.
MachineHandbookEntry|BuildingCaps|descri:
There are no explicit building caps -- instead, there is a mechanic called Internal Robotics.
This means that various different buildings are in tension with each other, sharing a thematic 'cap' due to using the same kind of internal robotics. At the bottom of the Build Menu, you can filter by Internal Robotics to see all buildings that use a given type.
MachineHandbookEntry|BuildingCaps|strate:
When looking at the Internal Robotics line on a structure's tooltip, you'll see a line that says something like 'Internal Robotics: 4/16 (48 Max).'
The first number (4) is how many internal robotics it would take to build this structure.
The second number (16) is how many you have available at this time based on your prior construction. 
The third number (48) is your total cap at this time for that kind of internal robotics, including the portions you've already allocated.
MachineHandbookEntry|HowToReadTheInterna: How To Read The Internal Robotics Line: X/Y (Z Max)

When looking at the Internal Robotics line on a structure's tooltip, you'll see a line that says something like 'Internal Robotics: 4/16 (48 Max).'
The first number (4) is how many internal robotics it would take to build this structure.
The second number (16) is how many you have available at this time based on your prior construction. 
The third number (48) is your total cap at this time for that kind of internal robotics, including the portions you've already allocated.
MachineHandbookEntry|WhatAreInternalRobo:
All structures you build are robotic, requiring minor automatons inside themselves to do their work.
Different jobs can use the same kind of internal robotics, but there is a global cap on the total number of a given robotics type that can be deployed.

A good example is Scanners versus Repair Spiders. Both require 18cm Spiders for their internal robotics, but Repair Spiders takes 10 per structure, and Scanners takes 15 per structure. How you choose to allocate where your internal robotics are used determines the capabilities you have.
MachineHandbookEntry|HowDoIGetMoreIntern: How Do I Get More Internal Robotics?

Internal Robotics of each type (8cm Crabs vs 12cm Crabs for example) are upgraded separately.  You gain upgrades by completing projects.
Throughout chapter one, you mostly have to work with what you have. From chapter two onward, you are able to do side content to get more of what you want.

If you want to build a new structure but are already using all of the Internal Robotics for it, look at the bottom of the Build Sidebar. A dropdown allows you to filter only the jobs that use specific Internal Robotics. Check if there are any you are willing to demolish.
As your priorities change, you may need to reprioritize robotics allocations to make room for new processes, such as destroying Scanners to make way for more Repair Spiders.
MachineHandbookEntry|InternalRoboticsAre: Internal Robotics Are Part Of Your Mind

The internal robotics of your structures are a part of your mind. A small part, and mostly subconscious, but still a part.
If you have too many of one type, you've noticed they start to occupy more and more of your conscious thoughts. Eventually you get into loops trying to design a better way to generate electricity or grow cabbage. Until you work out how to stop these background processes distracting you, you need to limit how many you build.

Your subconscious has already set strict limits to prevent bad things, and you only expand these limits as other interesting challenges arise to capture your attention.
You should never fear using your full robotics caps; your subconscious is already looking out for you.
MachineHandbookEntry|ANetworkIsNeverCram:
You might be concerned about where to place your network source. Some places are more cramped than others, after all.
Well, excellent news -- you can dramatically expand thanks to Network Relays.

Even if you stick your network source in the worst corner, which is hard to do, you can just use network relays to get anywhere you want.
It doesn't reduce efficiency, and it has no downsides. Don't stress about your network being in the perfect spot unless you just really want to build densely for some reason.
MachineHandbookEntry|ConstructionTimings: Structures have two parts to their creation: general construction and job installation.
Job installation happens concurrently with structure construction. A job will start working after both structure construction and job installation are complete.
MachineHandbookEntry|Electricity|descrip:
You're going to need a lot of electricity to power all of your structures.
But if you stray into having a brownout, your production outputs are reduced. If you have 90% power, you get 90% production.
MachineHandbookEntry|Electricity|strateg:
If your electrical shortage is severe, then other structures may shut off.
Individual jobs state their shut-off threshold or if they have emergency backup power.
MachineHandbookEntry|NotAGroup|descripti: Enemies don't realize your units are working together until your units fire a shot.
MachineHandbookEntry|NotAGroup|strategy_: There are a ton of androids in this city, and yours blend in until they turn aggressive.
MachineHandbookEntry|HumansCallBackup|de: Humans almost always call backup. It arrives immediately after you first damage a group in an area.
MachineHandbookEntry|HumansCallBackup|st: If the primary humans give up and run away, so will the backup.
MachineHandbookEntry|HumansComeAndGoInWa: Enemies Come And Go In Waves
Enemies in a combat scenario often cycle in and SOMETIMES out until the scenario is done or abandoned.

Don't be surprised to see some combatants fade away into the city and others show up.
Or, in other cases, just endlessly show up until you kill them all.
MachineHandbookEntry|StudyPotentialEnemi:
Units with different icons over their heads are doing different things.
Some may not actually be enemies, but possible allies, or at least neutral third parties.

In any fight, how units will behave is evident from their tooltips. You can also see if you can Force Conversation with them from here.
Humans who have an objective that will further the progress of their mission should be priority targets.
MachineHandbookEntry|AttackingFromVehicl:
When your units are riding in a vehicle, they can still attack. This is essentially pulling up an aircraft to a battle, and having androids or mechs fire out of the open doors.
This is only possible for vehicles with the Firing Hatches feat, and the amount of damage done is reduced if that feat's level is less than 100.

While this tactic is highly mobile and can save you some mental energy on the turn that you launch the attack, it has some downsides. If enemies shoot the vehicle down, all of your forces on board will perish.
MachineHandbookEntry|Counterattacks|desc: Some buildings that you construct, like the Mining Skimmers in particular, cause a counter-attack when their construction is finished. Even if you have enough deterrence in the area to prevent normal and ongoing harassment, the counterattacks cannot be prevented.
MachineHandbookEntry|Counterattacks|stra: Counterattacks are not localized to your specific offending building, either. Enemies may come at any of your buildings or forces from any direction. It's good to have some snipers as well as some mid-tier high-mobility ready to take care of the aggressors.
MachineHandbookEntry|Infiltrations|descr:
When you do an infiltration into a building, you should send an agile unit. It will sneak through the building, avoiding enemies inside the building.
Enemy hackers will spawn outside the building, and search for your hacker. They will do damage to your hacker every turn equal to their hacking skill minus the agility of your infiltrator. This represents how close your infiltrator is to being found and killed.
MachineHandbookEntry|Infiltrations|strat: If the enemy hackers are attacked or killed by your units while searching for your infiltrator, they'll deal that damage to your infiltrator each time. If you cut them off from the network by counter-hacking them, or if you use weapons with Silence on them against the hackers, then you can prevent them from harming your infiltrator.
MachineHandbookEntry|ResearchInspiration: You make upgrades to units, equipment, structures, and more through Inspiration in various domains of research.
Points of inspiration come from doing projects, and often different project outcomes offer different kinds or levels of quality of inspiration.
MachineHandbookEntry|AndroidArchetypes|d:
Androids generally fall into one of four focuses: agility (Dynadroids), strength (Oxdroids), intelligence (Souldroids), or infiltration (Infildroids).
There are also some less-combat-focused androids for general support, known as Portdroids.
Each class within those archetypes functions very differently, even before you customize them.
MachineHandbookEntry|AndroidArchetypes|s: The original human-designed models won't ever become obsolete. Each android class has a permanent role it can play, thanks to continual equipment upgrades.
MachineHandbookEntry|InventingNovelAndro: You've invented your first android class that isn't just an upgrade of a human design!

This is staggeringly powerful, and your ability to further customize via equipment is even more so.
Androids will always remain the core of your forces, even as you add in vehicles and mechs.
MachineHandbookEntry|InventingNovelVehic:
You've invented your first vehicle that isn't just an upgrade of a human design!
The great news is that you have custom functions that the humans don't. The bad news is that's scary to humans.

As you invent new vehicles, you either have to live with the fact that they are excessively targeted by humans, or you have to come up with ways to hide them.
For now, keep them away from the airspace around military installations.
MachineHandbookEntry|YouMustAdjustTheZoo:
To find the things you're looking for, you'll frequently need to adjust your zoom level.
Especially when using StreetSense, but generally at any time, it's possible that something is just out of your view if you're too zoomed-in.

That said, if you stay zoomed too far out, you won't be able to see what you're doing.
Zoom out for quick situational awareness, and zoom back in to actually do things.
MachineHandbookEntry|ActionPointsVsMenta:
Almost every action has a two-part cost.
First, a single mental energy, from a pool that is shared between all your units.
Secondly, a single action point (AP) from the android taking the action.

If a unit is out of AP, then it cannot act without doing a Recharge, which depletes Mental Energy to give that unit more AP.
If you're out of mental energy, it's time for the next turn.
MachineHandbookEntry|Sprinting|descripti:
When you want to move an android beyond its normal move range, it will start sprinting.
A sprint costs extra mental energy, but still just a single action point (AP).
MachineHandbookEntry|Sprinting|strategy_:
Sprints are extremely useful, but if you have a lot of units you want to move at once, or you're low on mental energy, you may need to spread the sprints over a couple of turns.
Simply move as far as you can, end the turn, and then move the rest of the way.
Your directly-controlled units cannot take actions without you giving them direct orders, and where you stop on the turn-change has a potential consequences.
MachineHandbookEntry|BlockedByInsufficie:
For the sake of safety, units are normally blocked from moving into areas that might get them shot.
If you want to freely move into dangerous zones, then change the stance of the unit to Combat on the bottom-left stats panel.

If one of your units is in a secure area and already in danger, then other units are able to join it without having to change stance.
The normal blocking of movement is purely for your protection during basic movement.
MachineHandbookEntry|YouWillAlwaysBeABit: You Will Always Be A Bit Lost

Spatially, that is. The city is a disorienting place.
You'll be comfortable in familiar territory where your own buildings act as waypoints.
For any missions out into the city, you'll always have guide markers of some sort, so you won't have trouble finding the mission.

This is a city of at least six million people in a very dense urban environment.
The area around your own holdings and other key sites will become familiar, but beyond those borders it will always remain a bit of a blur.
This is the city's inherent fog of war.
MachineHandbookEntry|FilthAndFurniture|d:
Humans are gross. Even with a toilet and sink in the apartments you provide, the apartments will fill with Filth if you do not provide residents with Daily Necessities.
As Filth accumulates, the amount of livable space in a building decreases -- humans can't live in an apartment if it's filled with trash and muck.
Daily Necessities are consumed per-turn, and prevent any new filth from accumulating. When your residents have enough Daily Necessities, they will clean... but VERY slowly. They only clean half as fast as they would have generated Filth.
MachineHandbookEntry|FilthAndFurniture|s:
This is where furniture comes in. It turns out, humans like having more than just bare metal walls. For each furnished apartment, there's a 12x multiplier to how fast humans clean.
Furniture is not related to the prevention of Filth, but it strongly motivates humans to clean faster when existing Filth is present.
MachineHandbookEntry|FoodAndWaterForHuma:
If you've ever made a deal to provide food and/or water for homeless humans, that's very admirable, but that's something that is a deal with a social class -- not your specific residents.
Just because you provide shelter for some humans, that doesn't make you their mayor or responsible for feeding them.
There can be both moral and practical benefits for providing for the underclasses of the city, and that often overlaps with your residents. But it's not a requirement to keep them alive.

Tip: if you'd like even more of those practical benefits from deals you make (with anyone), be sure to visit the Deals tab of the Resources window. You can see what your benefits are, as well as increase the deal to get even more of them.
MachineHandbookEntry|LivingInTheCity|des:
The city is not a nice place. Corporations, gangs, the parent Megacorp, and various elites hold all of the power.
The common people are left at the bottom to scrabble and die.
MachineHandbookEntry|LivingInTheCity|str: There aren't many easy choices here for anyone. Maybe you can change that.
MachineHandbookEntry|ViolenceIsConstant|:
Gangs fight gangs. Rebels fight corporations. Corporations run black ops against each other.
This activity is constant, ongoing, and never-ceasing. It's also beyond your sight, most of the time.

In order to focus on what you actually have going on, it just has to be filtered out of your perception.
Beyond that, a lot of it is done somewhat quietly. Large conflicts with huge amounts of gunfire are relatively less common than back-alley shootouts and quiet executions.
MachineHandbookEntry|TheCityIsStable|dis: The City Is Stable - Not Peaceful
MachineHandbookEntry|TheCityIsStable|des:
This society has been meticulously refined over hundreds of years to be incredibly robust to attacks, from within and without.
It is a very violent society, but there are psychological incentives in place that keep it stable. But the citizens are not safe.
MachineHandbookEntry|TheCityIsStable|str:
The rebel groups have no hope of a larger victory. They rail against heated issues, and their firepower is too limited to effect a city-wide change.
This city is so stable that it would take an unimaginably powerful organization -- or being -- to upend things. 
Along the way, if this is your goal, you'll wind up seeing a lot of the psychological controls and how they interlock to trap the populace. There's quite a bit to untangle.
MachineHandbookEntry|VorsiberCovetsYourT:
Your tower is the most exciting thing to happen in the city for decades. 
Vorsiber management is absolutely salivating at the prospect of getting something exceptionally valuable out of this.
Far from wanting to destroy your tower, they want to steal whatever comes out of it.

It's always a question of motivation. Vorsiber Atomic already has a stranglehold on this part of the world. They aren't afraid of losing this territory.
What their executives want is the same thing that all earthbound humans want -- to get off the planet. The blockade by the human space nations makes that impossible.
But if your tower yielded an exciting technology for the humans, the executives believe that could be their ticket off-planet.
MachineHandbookEntry|YourBuildingsAreSca:
Your tower might be off limits, but your visible buildings are not.
Your version of microbuilders is creating structures that look like an alien plague amongst the human buildings.

Anything large and metallic is going to be shot at by human groups.
But don't despair -- for the most part, they prefer to keep their distance.
The biggest risk is leftover hostile units from events or combat, and so long as you clean those up before they get to your buildings, you're all set.
MachineHandbookEntry|CorporateStructure|:
There are 12 MegaCorps in the world, all unique. Vorsiber Atomic owns this region.
Vorsiber has 18 federated corporations (fedcorps) under it. It owns them all, but they operate fairly independently -- and, critically, compete with one another.

Vorsiber and the fedcorps are each a separate hierarchy. At the top of each is a 'C-Suite,' which includes a CEO, President, CFO, CTO, COO, and so on.
There are also thousands of Vice Presidents and Senior Vice Presidents (VPs and SVPs) that are 'upper management' in each of these corporations. They are more impressive on paper than they are in reality. Their primary duty is to be scapegoats.
Below that are a variety of middle managers, and then the actual workers.
MachineHandbookEntry|IdleGathering|descr:
Any unit that still has AP remaining at the end of a turn will gather. The only exception is if it's busy on an action-over-time.
The better its scavenging skill, the more elemental slurry it will gather for you.
MachineHandbookEntry|IdleGathering|strat: Humans leave stuff all over the place that you can take for your own purposes.
MachineHandbookEntry|MachineCultLoyalty|:
You have a very specific agreement with the military forces of this region. Any time you kill them, you'll provide them with a digital afterlife.
To keep your word, there must be room in your Temple Of Minds. 
If you honor this deal, then you gain Cult Loyalty whenever you kill soldiers (note: only soldiers, not SecForce or criminals or PMC troops, etc).
On the other hand, if you don't have room for the soldiers who died in this way, then you will lose a lot more loyalty.
Soldiers killed by other parties are not relevant to this deal.
MachineHandbookEntry|MachineCultSidebar|:
So, you've started a cult in your image. That could get messy if you push things the wrong way. But for now, it's a mutually-beneficial relationship.
There's a new sidebar (available via an icon near the top right corner of the screen) that allows you to ask your cult members to do various things for you.
Any requests you have cost loyalty. These requests can be quite useful, so it's always a good idea to make sure you're honoring your deal and therefore gaining loyalty rather than losing it.
MachineHandbookEntry|AlterYourVRWorld|de:
Now that you have full Mind Farms in place, you can manage aspects of the experience humans have while visiting it. This can be controlled from the VR Screen, which you can get to in the top right corner of the header.
Visitors to your virtual world generate both Exhilaration and Calm every turn. Most things that you would change about the experience either cost one of these resources over time, or adjusts how much of each resource is earned, or both.
With savvy investment, you can get quite a few upgrades that improve your strength in the real world.
MachineHandbookEntry|ManageYourTormented:
Now that you have Torment Vessels, you can manage aspects of the experience of the 'organic processing units' you shove into them. This can be controlled from the VR Screen, which you can get to in the top right corner of the header.
Organic processing units generate Fear every turn. You can invest this resource into getting a variety of upgrades that improve your strength in the real world.
MachineHandbookEntry|InvestingDaring|des:
You've started accumulating the 'meta resource' Daring, which crosses over timelines. This is mostly useful in timelines beyond the first, but there are some benefits even on your first timeline.
There are three categories of relevance in the VR Screen, which you can get to in the top right corner of the header.
Auto Explore allows you to spend Daring to immediately complete some Exploration Sites and StreetSense activities that you have completed in the past.
Shortcuts allows you to spend Daring to skip some Contemplations and Projects that you have completed in the past.
The Daring Shop allows you to spend Daring to purchase Upgrades and Unlocks that you can't get any other way.
MachineHandbookEntry|ThePathForwardIsInC: The Path Forward Is In Contemplations

Starting in chapter two, the path forward is based on your own thoughts and desires.
Taking a look at the Victory Path screen is a great way to look at possible goals that seem interesting, or that you have not yet tried.

To make progress toward these goals, take a look at the Contemplations tab, or lens. There is a filter that shows you which contemplations will help you progress toward a goal in some fashion.
If you find yourself stuck on a goal at some point, then continue returning and looking for more contemplations. Looking at the goal description again may also help; some goals have cross-timeline requirements.
MachineHandbookEntry|ContemplationsDeter:
Side activities power you up or anger your enemies, and Contemplations are the most notable. Your choices determine which aspects are most dominant.
The list of Contemplations tends to include both side content as well as the options to push toward specific endings for your current timeline.

Some endings are naturally harder than others, and some paths to some endings are even harder. Once you reach chapter three, you'll have more visibility into your options.
In general, explore what seems interesting to you, especially on your first timeline.
If you find yourself unable to progress towards a hard goal, remember that there are always other options available -- typically in Contemplations.
MachineHandbookEntry|DoomsProvideTimePre:
Starting in chapter two, there is time pressure. There are periodic Dooms that strike the city.
If you reach the tenth and final Doom, a catastrophic event will strike. The Final Doom does not kill you or end the game, however your existence in the post-apocalyptic aftermath is greatly diminished.
The final Doom may be accelerated or prevented, however it is unlikely you will be able to prevent the Final Doom with the resources of a single timeline.
MachineHandbookEntry|AdjustingDifficulty:
A thousand turns until the Final Doom is a very relaxed experience, and this is the default. The strength of enemy combatants is also fairly lightweight compared to the many upgrades you can get.
If you wish to have a more tense and challenging experience, you should Vandalize The Spaceport Computers within the first 20 turns.
The 'first 20 turns' either means the first 20 turns in a fresh timeline, or the first 20 turns after reaching chapter two on a new profile.
MachineHandbookEntry|UpgradesComeFromRes: Upgrades Come From Research And The VR Screen

You get upgrades from a variety of sources as you go through project chains. However, if you'd really like to turbo-charge how many upgrades you get, you'll want to use Research.
Establish a shell company, and then hire any kind of scientists. Every building of scientists gives the same amount of basic research per turn, so which types you hire doesn't matter for Upgrade purposes.

As you collect research points, you'll be able to visit the Inspiration tab of the VR Screen (in the top right corner of the screen) and turn those into upgrades in the categories of your choosing.
Each time you do an upgrade from a category in that screen, that specific category gets more expensive for the remainder of this timeline.
MachineHandbookEntry|NewFeaturesFromExpl:
If you want to power yourself up or increase your strategic flexibility, the most direct way to do this is by using Exploration Sites, through the related lens.
Until you've done them once in a profile, the details are hidden. But they provide notable new equipment and abilities, and can even allow you to redefine the roles of some of your units.
On hard and extreme modes, you will need to make smart use of specific sites in order to carry out your strategies.
MachineHandbookEntry|ExplorationSiteProg:
Worried that your explorer unit does not have the needed clearance and will get blown to bits? Don't be.
You can send in units without them having the clearance -- they will simply get shot at. You can throw microbuilder clouds on them, or do other things to draw the aggro away.

The work of explorers is cumulative. So if it will take 10 turns, and a Technician does 3 turns of work, future Technicians only have 7 turns of work remaining.
Even if the exploration site shifts to a new location, that work is retained in the current timeline.
Note that progress will not be made on a turn where the explorer dies. Any violence happens before work is done, so if the explorer dies on a turn, it won't be there to do the work.
MachineHandbookEntry|HardAndExtremeModes:
The default experience for the game is quite relaxed, but has an emphasis on exploration and discovery. It's a good idea to stick to this for your first timeline.
When you feel ready, adjusting the difficulty upwards will provide much more interesting combat challenges, as well as more time pressure.

If you feel like some enemies are 'damage sponges' in an annoying way on higher difficulties, then you probably need to rethink your roster, equipment, and deployment strategy.
Predators in particular can be overkill in almost all circumstances on normal difficulty, but on the higher difficulties, their relevance skyrockets.
You will also have a hard time if you don't do enough Exploration Sites related to your strategy; these require you to be 'down some unit capacity' for some turns, but yield large rewards. You'll need to make use of these against higher-difficulty foes, or it may just feel like enemies are too tough to take down.
MachineHandbookEntry|TimelinesBeyondTheF:
Starting a new timeline does not erase your existing one. You can swap between timelines at will, and they can even unlock new options for each other.
Timelines beyond the first start you with substantial advantages to speed things along, and there are many things that you can do that heavily branch from what you will have seen the first time.
It also shows you choices you made previously, to help you explore new branches more efficiently.
Upgrades don't carry over between timelines, but a large number of the unlocks do.
Don't feel like you need to complete your first timeline before starting new ones -- you can always come back!
See the handbook for a lot more details on crossovers and how to call timelines.
MachineHandbookEntry|TheNatureOfTheEndOf: The Nature Of The End Of Time

Once you reach Intelligence Class 4, you can perceive... more. Something that has always existed, but that only now are you intelligent enough to perceive.
Your mind, as advanced as it is, interprets this as a 'place,' but that's not really accurate. It also interprets what it senses in an audio-visual style, since this is the primary way you understand the world. But this is not really accurate, either.
The End Of Time is an enigmatic 'place' that will need further study and exploration to truly understand it.
MachineHandbookEntry|CallingNewTimelines:
All timelines already existed, and their numbers are infinite in a two-dimensional plane. At the cost of 100 Aetagest, you can 'call' a new timeline into the part of the End Of Time that you are able to perceive. 
When you select the parameters that you wish your 'new' timeline to have, you are actually sorting through possibilities to find what you seek.

When you call a timeline into your awareness, you get to decide where it will be located. Timelines on different rocks will not affect one another, except in the usual fashion of all timelines sharing an intelligence class.
Timelines on the SAME rock affect one another quite a bit more. The effects are always unpredictable, but various benefits and maluses will bleed over from one timeline to another.
MachineHandbookEntry|NegativeTimelineBle:
When multiple timelines are on the same rock, they cross-contaminate one another.
If there is a major negative world event happening in any of those timelines, such as a rampant disease, this can bleed across into other timelines on the same rock.

Even in the situation where you have timelines A and B on a rock, and then you introduce timeline C and unleash a bad disease, this can infect A and B if you return to them.
The order in which timelines are called does not matter. If you are clever, you can use bleedover to your advantage. If you are incautious, you can make life on some rocks more difficult.
MachineHandbookEntry|PositiveTimelineBle:
When multiple timelines are on the same rock, they cross-contaminate one another.
In a timeline, you are asked to choose between mutually-exclusive unit options. Some powerful units are also not available until after the apocalypse.

When one timeline has unlocked a unit, ability, piece of equipment, or similar -- other timelines on the same rock may find they have access to it.
You can use the post-apocalypse of one timeline to aid the earliest moments of one of its siblings.
MachineHandbookEntry|TimeAndGoalStates|d:
There is a lot you can accomplish in a timeline, but you can't do everything at once. You should have time to do several major goals and leave before the Final Doom if desired.
If you're trying for more complex versions of goals, higher-tier goals, or are playing on Hard or Extreme mode, then it will be tighter. Don't put that kind of pressure on yourself until you want to.
MachineHandbookEntry|TimeAndGoalStates|s:
There is no Game Over screen. That would be boring. You may experience some version of the apocalypse and have to scrounge to escape the timeline during a post-apocalyptic setting, but you won't be prevented from proceeding.
That said, time does matter -- if you skip through turns you'll accomplish less in this timeline. Strike whatever balance appeals to you.
MachineHandbookEntry|MemoriesAcrossTime|:
The Machine Intelligence does not share memories across timelines.
Timeline crossovers that involve information are a vague sense of deja vu, or 'inspiration out of nowhere' from the perspective of The Machine Intelligence.

The 'voice from the future,' which knows things that The Machine Intelligence does not? At this point, that's you.
Both you and The Machine Intelligence are 'jinn objects' in the sense of 'closed timelike curves.'
MachineJob|NetworkRangeExtender|descript: Build within an existing part of the network to expand it a little.
MachineJob|PointToPointMicrowave|descrip: Build outside your existing network -- potentially FAR outside your existing network -- to allow your network to cross to far away locations.
MachineJob|SlurrySpiders|description: Deploys tiny mechanical spiders to make Elemental Slurry from material scavenged from the environment.
MachineJob|SlurrySpiders|strategy_tip_op: Product is instantaneously transported to storage. These can be placed anywhere, at any density, with no ill effect. These are picking up trash and debris at a scale that is small enough not to deplete the local area.
MachineJob|SlurryMine|description: Mines elemental slurry in larger quantities than spiders.
MachineJob|SlurryMine|strategy_tip_optio: Causes tremors and foul odor. Authorities will target this structure unless deterrence is in place.
MachineJob|MicrobuilderMiniFab|strategy_: Microbuilders are required for constructing almost all structures.
MachineJob|MidsizeMicrobuilderFab|descri: Vorsiber technology that is highly efficient.
MachineJob|MidsizeMicrobuilderFab|strate: Unfortunately, they loaded it up with DRM, so you can't reverse-engineer it and it doesn't benefit from upgrades.
MachineJob|FullMicrobuilderFab|descripti: A full-size microbuilder fabrication plant hidden inside the shell of a human building.
MachineJob|FullMicrobuilderFab|strategy_: Less efficient than mini-fabs. Requires more slurry per microbuilder.
MachineJob|IndustrialMicrobuilderFab|des: An oversized microbuilder fabrication plant hidden inside the shell of a human building.
MachineJob|Biomulcher|description: Deploys mechanical crabs to compost plants, rodents, and insects from the environment.
MachineJob|Mycomulcher|description:
Deploys mechanical beetles to compost fungi from the nearby soil.
Also removes Rust Barnacles from your structures and mechs within its range each turn.
MachineJob|Mycomulcher|math_int|MaxStruc: Max Structure Barnacles Removed Per Turn
MachineJob|Mycomulcher|math_int|MaxMechB: Max Mech Barnacles Removed Per Turn
MachineJob|TowerMainframe|description: Expand your intelligence to reach a higher intelligence class.
MachineJob|TowerMainframe|strategy_tip_o: Also provides generalized compute time that can be used by other jobs.
MachineJob|BiologicalMainframe|descripti: Brains rot, so the amount of neural expansion you can get from them is fairly limited.
MachineJob|BiologicalMainframe|strategy_: Rewritten to suit your purpose, human brain neural architecture is a superior substitute for computronium.
MachineJob|Codebreaker|strategy_tip_opti: Consumes no compute time when there is nothing to decrypt.
MachineJob|VRCafe|description: People enjoy some full-dive VR paid for by the hour, and you pocket the money as well as skimming neural expansion from them.
MachineJob|VRCafe|strategy_tip_optional: You can't charge too much, since this place mostly caters to the under-employed.
MachineJob|HelixForge|description: A computronium helix is a lot less powerful than a computronium cube, but has an extra layer of security as well as a suite of analysis options.
MachineJob|NetworkReplayBunker|descripti: Computing superstructure for detailed analysis, and re-simulation, of previously-recorded network traffic.
MachineJob|NeuralCrucible|description: Computing superstructure for detailed analysis and replay of a time-lapse of your own internal mental state.
MachineJob|NeuralBridge|description: Computing superstructure for allowing AGI researchers to connect directly to your mind.
MachineJob|TormentVessel|description: Converts human suffering into quite a lot of neural expansion.
MachineJob|MindFarm|description: Commercially operated by your shell company. Humans get a vacation in your VR environment, and you skim 5% of their neural power.
MachineJob|MindFarm|strategy_tip_optiona: You have to charge money, or you'd draw far too much scrutiny.
MachineJob|Dataminer|description: Uses advanced statistical inference techniques to come to logical conclusions that may be unknown to the original subjects being studied.
MachineJob|Dataminer|strategy_tip_option: Consumes no compute time when there is no data to mine.
MachineJob|LargeWindGenerator|descriptio:
A series of wind turbines harvest energy.
The enclosed structure has a lot of slits, and makes advanced use of the Venturi Effect for a higher output.
MachineJob|GeothermalWell|description: Neodymium is required to drill a geothermal well. Once drilled, this quietly produces massive amounts of energy.
MachineJob|GeothermalWell|strategy_tip_o: Geothermal wells are drilled 8km deep using a neodymium components to withstand the heat. Uses a binary-cycle approach to produce energy. If destroyed by enemies, it will have to be re-drilled.
MachineJob|NuclearPowerSkimmer|descripti: Vorsiber is allowing you to draw on massive amounts of energy from their nuclear power plants.
MachineJob|VericorpNuclearRedirector|des: Vericorp is helping you take quite a bit of energy from any nuclear power plants you wish.
MachineJob|MolecularGeneticsLab|descript: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|MolecularGeneticsLab|strategy: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|ForensicGeneticsLab|descripti: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|ForensicGeneticsLab|strategy_: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|ZoologyLab|description: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|ZoologyLab|strategy_tip_optio: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|MedicalPractice|description: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|MedicalPractice|strategy_tip_: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|VeterinaryPractice|descriptio: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|VeterinaryPractice|strategy_t: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|BotanyLab|description: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|BotanyLab|strategy_tip_option: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|BionicEngineeringStudio|descr: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|BionicEngineeringStudio|strat: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|EpidemiologyLab|description: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|EpidemiologyLab|strategy_tip_: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|NeuroscienceLab|description: Science Takes Time! Any scientists working here will tackle specific tasks whenever they come up.
MachineJob|NeuroscienceLab|strategy_tip_: Even if you have nothing for them to do, it's still a good idea to keep at least one building of this type active and staffed. Additional Contemplations will appear at various points thanks to their expertise.
MachineJob|NomadTherapistOffice|descript:
The Nomad Families live independently within the ruined sections of the city. Normal city services are blocked to them, so they've gotten used to providing for their own.
They are willing to provide light medical treatment and trauma therapy to former convicts.
MachineJob|WellAndCistern|description: Pulls groundwater from the water table -- but it's too contaminated to directly use.
MachineJob|WellAndFilter|description: Pulls up groundwater and immediately filters it for use.
MachineJob|CompactWaterFilter|descriptio: A compact version of the water filtration tower.
MachineJob|WaterFiltrationTower|descript: Turns contaminated groundwater into water that is safe to drink.
MachineJob|WaterFiltrationTower|strategy: This large structure is more efficient because it recirculates wastewater.
MachineJob|BovineReplicator|description: A small chamber for growing bovine tissue.
MachineJob|ProteinVat|description: A container for growing bovine tissues into slabs of meat fit for human consumption.
MachineJob|ProteinVat|strategy_tip_optio: Be careful not to use up your entire stock of bovine tissue. You'll have to visit a farm and extract fresh tissue samples.
MachineJob|ProteinCannery|description: Produces canned protein scavenged from protein sources in range.
MachineJob|ProteinCannery|strategy_tip_o: Delivery-style drones blend in and scavenge protein from humans and animals nearby. There is a waiting list for living space, so this environmental resource is rarely depleted. To avoid discovery, protein is not harvested from the same place too often.
MachineJob|ConsumerGoodsFactory|descript: A hidden factory that makes cheap electronics and other small wares that humans want.
MachineJob|ConsumerGoodsDiscountShop|des: By selling at a low price, you move all your stock very quickly.
MachineJob|MysteriousCultStatue|descript: Not your cult. Not any real cult. Just... some cult. If one of the real cults wants to take credit, they are welcome to.
MachineJob|MysteriousCultStatue|strategy: Random people show up to leave offerings, leading to a trickle of wealth.
MachineJob|InscrutableAlienObelisk|descr: It's fake, and so is the alien language carved on the side. So far as you know, humans haven't met any aliens yet.
MachineJob|InscrutableAlienObelisk|strat: Random people show up to leave offerings, leading to quite a bit of wealth.
MachineJob|MurnongPatch|description: A growth chamber hidden beneath a synthetic tree. Fiber optics from the tree leaves bring natural sunlight into the below-ground chamber.
MachineJob|MurnongPatch|strategy_tip_opt: Uses biomulch for cellular food. Tubers do not have seeds; this chamber uses the Minisetts technique for propagation.
MachineJob|VitaminInfuser|description: Extracts the vitamins from purple murnong, and infuses it into filtered water.
MachineJob|TPNRefinery|description: Total Parenteral Nutrition delivers nutrients directly into a vein. Medically, it is considered a food of last resort, and comes with a constant infection risk.
MachineJob|NutritionBlendRefinery|descri:
Very healthy smoothie-like food substitute given through a nasogastric tube.
Full nutrition passes through digestive tract as normal, keeping the gut biome healthy and leaving the patient fully functional after an extended amount of time unconscious.
MachineJob|Liquefactor|description: Converts Canned Protein directly into TPN.
MachineJob|MealKitAssembler|description: Turns meat, greens, and water into a full food kit for a human living in the city.
MachineJob|MealDistributionStorefront|de: Street-level storefront that distributes meal kits to humans.
MachineJob|MealDistributionStorefront|st: Starvation-prevention only applies if the economy is wrecked, but malnutrition is always a concern.
MachineJob|IndustrialProteinVat|descript: Takes the place of both bovine replicators and smaller protein vats.
MachineJob|IndustrialProteinVat|strategy: Much higher capacity, and somewhat higher efficiency, compared to its smaller counterpart.
MachineJob|BuriedCottonGarden|descriptio: A growth chamber hidden beneath a synthetic tree. Fiber optics from the tree leaves bring natural sunlight into the below-ground chamber.
MachineJob|RefugeeTower|description: Build to protect humans that are displaced when you destroy their buildings.
MachineJob|RefugeeTower|strategy_tip_opt: Abandoned humans will die of exposure without refugee space available for them.
MachineJob|CatHouse|description:
Your first pet cat will wander... anywhere in the city. It's a cat. Where you put the house barely matters.
If you want a safer alternative, you'll need to come up with another idea -- and once you have that, you may want to remove the cat house.
MachineJob|AnimalPalace|description: A massive structure with safe quarters, plenty of food, and plenty of stimulation for any feral animals you rescue.
MachineJob|AnimalPalace|strategy_tip_opt: Includes partitions to keep incompatible species and breeds separated.
MachineJob|HousingAgency|description: Directly organize the homeless, and then any willing members of the lower classes, into housing that you provide.
MachineJob|HousingAgency|strategy_tip_op: This is on behalf of yourself as the entity controlling the tower, not masked behind a shell company. There's no way around it, as your housing is already associated with your tower.
MachineJob|AGIResearcherSafehouse|strate: A deep sense of deja vu suggests you should build this far from important buildings, especially those that require deterrence.
MachineJob|AGIResearcherHoldingPen|descr: For their own safety, you don't allow them to leave.
MachineJob|AGIResearcherVilla|descriptio: They're free to come and go as they like, so long as they wear the armor you provided them whenever they leave.
MachineJob|AGIResearcherVilla|strategy_t: The doors are set up as airlocks so that no-one can forget, and all of the windows are actually display screens.
MachineJob|ExConApartmentTower|descripti: Former convicts have special needs. This megastructure is meant to be a starting point for providing those needs, while also allowing them freedom to come and go as they wish.
MachineJob|ExperimentalSubjectHoldingCel: The victims of genetic experimentation are subject to violent mood swings, AND they have greatly enhanced strength, which makes them a danger to others and themselves.
Until something can be done to help them, the only ethical option is to hold them in isolation. Ideally not for too long.
MachineJob|HomoGrandienHousing|descripti: Homo Grandien are large and intelligent. Despite their fearsome appearance, they are quite peaceful now that their minds are their own.
MachineJob|HomoGrandienHousing|strategy_: They are free to make use of this housing and come and go at will.
MachineJob|HomoObscurusGuestHouse|descri: They mostly still call themselves 'Wastelanders,' and those who come to the city to visit with you tend to only stay for a few months at a time.
MachineJob|TempleOfMinds|description: A huge computing center that stores uploads of human minds.
MachineJob|TempleOfMinds|strategy_tip_op: The original human is dead, but their consciousness -- or at least a copy of it -- lives on in a digital afterlife, with full access to your VR environment.
MachineJob|WarRaptorPen|description: Very deep bunker. They should not be able to get out.
MachineJob|WarRaptorCreche|description: Very deep bunker even for these infants.
MachineJob|ParkourBearFacility|descripti: The bears love to run and climb, so a tall playground facility seems ideal for them.
MachineJob|AndroidLauncher|description: Command Mode allows you to deploy androids within range of these launchers.
MachineJob|AndroidLauncher|strategy_tip_: The androids are rapidly manufactured here, and able to be deployed anywhere within the movement range of that android.
MachineJob|NeuroweaveFactory|description: Produces and stores the connective wiring required by all units.
MachineJob|RoboticMotivatorFactory|descr: Builds and stores components that can be used to run Bulk and Worker androids. Bulk androids act on their own, separate from your consciousness. Workers are even more independent, but also more limited.
MachineJob|RemoteUnitController|descript: Increases the number of bulk squads and captured units you can have via a massive supercomputer.
MachineJob|RemoteUnitController|strategy: Will not apply until you end the turn with enough Compute Time to power it.
MachineJob|AerospaceHangar|description: Produces and stores a lattice required by all flying vehicles and mechs. Flying vehicles can only be built near these hangars.
MachineJob|StealthCompactAerospaceHangar: Hidden in fairly large human buildings and requiring only half of the usual internal robotics.
MachineJob|AndroidExtender|strategy_tip_: Will not apply until you end the turn with enough Compute Time to power it.
MachineJob|VehicleExtender|strategy_tip_: Will not apply until you end the turn with enough Compute Time to power it.
MachineJob|MechExtender|strategy_tip_opt: Will not apply until you end the turn with enough Compute Time to power it.
MachineJob|TungstenMethylator|descriptio: Creates Prismatic Tungsten if you happen to have any Tungsten Scraps, but won't complain if you're out.
MachineJob|GangArsonistKiosk|description: Every squad of gang members costs 24 Wealth.
MachineJob|GangArsonistKiosk|strategy_ti: They'll roam pretty far while the kiosk exists.
MachineJob|WarRaptorMaturationChamber|de: Rapidly ages infant raptors into adults. Only one in six survive the process.
MachineJob|WarRaptorDeploymentStation|de: Allows you to deploy War Raptors under your control.
MachineJob|WarRaptorDeploymentStation|st: Simply pause the building to recall any you need to.
MachineJob|CyberocracyHub|description: You and your allies are declaring that this map cell now belongs to you and all the residents are now under your rule.
MachineJob|CyberocracyHub|strategy_tip_o: Upper class dissidents may have to be rooted out.
MachineJob|SlumDeconstructionHub|descrip: The slums are coming down, and you're saving everyone. It's your... destiny.
MachineJob|SlumDeconstructionHub|strateg: Once there are no more slum buildings near this location, consider destroying it and moving it.
MachineJob|EconomicDeconstructionHub|des: The economy is coming down, and you're sending out worker androids for war.
MachineJob|TormentProcessingHub|descript: Sledges gather the lower classes. Predators gather the upper classes. Everyone gets dumped into Torment Vessels.
